title: fix(driver-sql): give Field.datetime one UTC storage form per dialect (#3912, #3942)
body:
Closes #3912. Closes #3942. Closes #3928.

## The reported bug

Any window filter on a `Field.datetime` column returned an empty set on SQLite — a dashboard `dateRange: last_30_days` on `created_date` read 0 while 29 matching rows existed.

## Root cause

There was never a storage *convention*, only a description of what better-sqlite3 happened to do with a bound JS `Date`. Nothing enforced it — `formatInput` deliberately left `datetime` untouched — so the form was decided by whichever writer got there first:

- a JS `Date` (seed loader, import, server-side code) → INTEGER epoch ms
- a REST/JSON write → ISO **TEXT**, because JSON has no `Date` type
- a `defaultValue: 'NOW()'` slot → ISO TEXT
- the platform's own `created_at` / `updated_at` → ISO TEXT, on **every** object

One column held both forms while the read path coerced comparands to epoch ms purely from the *declared* type. On SQLite's type ordering (`INTEGER < TEXT`) a two-sided window collapsed to zero rows, and a one-sided `>=` matched every TEXT row regardless of the bound.

## What changed

`Field.datetime` now has one canonical instant per dialect, produced by one function (`canonicalUtcDatetime`) applied on write **and** to every filter comparand, so the two sides of a comparison cannot disagree about shape.

| dialect | storage | why |
|---|---|---|
| SQLite | `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ` text | lexicographic order **is** chronological order, so range filters and `ORDER BY` read the column directly and can use an index; `strftime` parses it, so the bucket expression needs no CASE; it is what `formatOutput` already presented; it matches the `Field.date` convention; and it was already the majority of rows on disk |
| Postgres | `timestamptz` (unchanged) | already correct — the fix here is on the write/comparand side |
| MySQL | `DATETIME(3)` | replaces `TIMESTAMP`: no 2038 ceiling, milliseconds kept, no session-timezone conversion |

An epoch integer was the alternative considered and rejected: it forces an expression wrapper on every temporal predicate — moving the cost rather than removing it — and it is the minority form on disk, so the migration would be larger.

## The other dialects were measured, not assumed

Against a real PostgreSQL 16 (`TimeZone = Asia/Shanghai`) and MariaDB 10.11 (`default_time_zone = '+08:00'`, process on `America/New_York`):

**Postgres** had no storage mix — `table.timestamp` creates `timestamptz` — but the same family of bug, quieter. A zone-naive write was resolved against the *server's* timezone and stored 8 hours off, and an un-anchored `YYYY-MM-DD` comparand meant the server's local midnight, so the identical query over the identical instant put a row on a **different calendar day** than SQLite did. Making the comparand rule dialect-independent fixes both; no migration needed.

**MySQL** was worst, and included a regression this branch introduced mid-way. MySQL accepts neither the `T` separator nor the `Z` suffix in a datetime literal, so the canonical form fails the statement outright. An ISO comparand or REST/JSON write had *always* failed that way — datetime writes over REST were broken on MySQL before any of this — and canonicalising the write path extended it to `Date` writes too. Baseline before this branch: ISO rejected, `Date` accepted but truncated to whole seconds, zone-naive stored 12 hours off (host zone and server zone compounding), nothing outside 1970..2038 storable.

Resolved by keeping the logical canon and changing only the physical spelling: `DATETIME(3)`, a connection pinned to UTC on both the mysql2 and the server layer, and a MySQL-spelled bind carrying the same UTC wall clock.

## Migration

Existing rows converge at schema sync — `backfillCanonicalDatetimes` on SQLite, `migrateMysqlDatetimeColumns` on MySQL. The SQLite one is a single `UPDATE` per column whose SET expression **is** the same expression the read paths use, so the migration cannot drift from the repair it retires; `col IS NOT <canonical>` is the whole `WHERE`, which is null-safe and type-aware, so epoch rows match, canonical rows are skipped, and unparseable values fall through unchanged rather than being destroyed. One scan, zero writes, idempotent.

Both are allowed to fail. They log, mark nothing, and the read paths keep their repair expression — so an un-migrated column still compares and buckets **correctly**, just unindexed. Query correctness must never be contingent on a migration having run, and the repair stays permanently for external/unmanaged tables (ADR-0015) that never get one.

Worth stating plainly: neither migration can repair instants the old timezone-ambiguous write path recorded wrongly. That information is gone. They preserve what is on disk.

## Testing

- New SQLite suites: every input shape folds to one stored string; `ORDER BY` is chronological across alternating write shapes; the backfill converges, is idempotent, preserves junk, and returns **identical rows before and after** (a migration must not be observable as a change in results). 13 of 16 cases in the legacy-storage suite fail without the change.
- Two opt-in live-server suites, `OS_TEST_POSTGRES_URL` and `OS_TEST_MYSQL_URL` — CI provisions no server, so they skip by default. Each asserts it is pointed at a **non-UTC** server so it cannot pass vacuously. 3 of 5 Postgres cases and 10 of 13 MySQL cases fail without the change.
- Suites that pinned the old mixed-storage premise now assert the new invariant, with the legacy forms moved to a `LegacyStorageDriver` test double — seeded raw with the canonical marker cleared, the honest simulation of a database whose backfill has not run.
- `pnpm build` + `pnpm test` green (132 tasks) on the merge with current `main`.

## Also in scope

**#3928** (datetime `ORDER BY` mis-sorted on mixed storage) is closed by construction rather than by a sort-side fix — the mixed form no longer exists, and fixed-width UTC text sorts correctly *through an index*, which the expression-sort alternative would have given up.

## Notes for review

- `isEpochStoredDatetime` is renamed to `needsLegacyDatetimeRepair`. It is `protected`, and the old name described a storage convention that no longer exists.
- ADR-0053 recorded "datetime stays stored as UTC epoch ms" as Phase 1 step 4; addendum **D-B1..D-B4** revises it with the measurements above.
- The merge with `main` resolved one adjacent-addition conflict against the deferred-DDL work (#3917). The interaction is correct as-is: the convergence hooks sit after the `if (this.deferredDdl) continue` gate, so `os migrate plan` performs no data rewrite or `ALTER`, and `flushDeferredSchemaDdl` re-enters `initObjects` with the deferral disarmed so `apply` runs them.
- **Known gap, filed separately:** `os migrate plan` will not *list* these convergence steps, because `PendingSchemaWork.kind` is an exported union covering only `create_table` / `add_columns`. Extending it plus the CLI renderer inside this PR would collide with #3917's just-landed work, so it is filed rather than bundled.
